entry.evidence: Humboldt Glacier, northern Greenland, has retreated and accelerated through the 21st century, raising concerns that it could be a significant contributor to future sea-level rise

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text with §-locators; PDF for figures)

steps.action: Report published observations that Humboldt has lost the most grounded ice of any GrIS outlet glacier, with retreat concentrated on its fast northern terminus over a deepening trough.
steps.quote: Humboldt has lost the greatest area of grounded ice since 1992 of any GrIS outlet glacier

steps.action: Pose the aim of estimating Humboldt Glacier's sea-level contribution for 2007-2100 and assessing its sources of uncertainty.
steps.quote: to estimate the SLR contribution from Humboldt Glacier from 2007–2100 and assess sources of uncertainty

steps.action: Use the authors' own three-dimensional, first-order Stokes, thermomechanically coupled MALI model on a 1-10 km variable-resolution regional mesh.
steps.quote: using the MPAS-Albany Land Ice (MALI; Model for Prediction Across Scales) model (Hoffman et al., 2018)

steps.action: Invert 2007-2008 winter velocities, with BedMachine v4 geometry, for the spatial basal friction parameter mu (q = 1/3) to build the 2007 initial condition.
steps.quote: We use a PDE-constrained (partial differential equation) adjoint optimization method to solve for the basal friction parameter μ

steps.action: Select three ISMIP6 climate forcings (MIROC5 and HadGEM2 RCP8.5, CNRM-CM6 SSP5-8.5) to represent medium, strong and midrange CMIP6 forcing.
steps.quote: We also include the CNRM-CM6 (Centre National de Recherches Meteorologiques Climate Model version 6) SSP5-8.5 forcing

steps.action: Treat the basal friction law exponent q as unknown, with candidate values from 1/10 to 1 that span the commonly used linear and 1/3 laws.
steps.quote: which is not known a priori and cannot be determined from a single snapshot in time

steps.action: Check that recalculating mu for each q from the optimized basal traction reproduces the optimized 2007 velocity (Fig. S2).
steps.quote: This relation yields very nearly the same velocity as the optimization for the initial condition (Fig. S2), which validates our recalculation of μ

steps.action: Run a decade of hindcasts (winter 2007-2008 to 2017-2018) for each q, imposing the observed mean retreat rate, to compute each exponent's predicted 2017 velocity field.
steps.quote: [...] of q considered, we impose a spatially variable calving front retreat rate that matches the mean observed retreat rate

steps.action: Compare modeled with observed 2017-2018 velocities as RMS misfits in four velocity bands (Fig. 3).
steps.quote: We calculate the root mean square error in the modeled velocities from the observed 2017–2018 winter velocities divided into four bands

steps.action: Select 1/7 <= q <= 1/5 as the calibrated range, rejecting q = 1/4 (the global-misfit optimum) and the commonly used 1/3-1 because they fit the fast terminus region poorly.
steps.quote: We find that 1 / 7 ≤ q ≤ 1 / 5 yields reasonable agreement to the 2017–2018 velocities in the fastest-flowing parts

steps.action: Test the q calibration against other velocity-band definitions (Fig. S3) and repeat it with 2015-2016 velocities and margin (Fig. S4).
steps.quote: we tested the sensitivity of the calibration to our choice of velocity bands and found it to be relatively insensitive (Fig. S3)

steps.action: After preliminary runs grew a sizable ice shelf, add a quadratic sub-shelf melt parameterization (Jourdain et al. 2020) alongside the grounded undercutting law.
steps.quote: In preliminary model runs, we found that the modeled glacier develops a sizable ice shelf by the middle of the 21st century

steps.action: Build 3D thermal forcing from Oceans Melting Greenland CTD/AXCTD profiles and tune gamma0 for each forcing to give a mean sub-shelf melt of 20 m/yr.
steps.quote: We then tune γ 0 in the TF–melt relationship to obtain mean melt rates of 20 m yr - 1 beneath floating ice

steps.action: Revise calving auxiliaries: drop the immediate calving of floating ice (which gave too rapid retreat), adopt von Mises calving with low sigma_max, and impose an ad hoc 3 km/yr calving-rate cap after preliminary runs ran away.
steps.quote: We found it necessary to impose a 3 km yr - 1 upper limit on the calving rate following Choi et al. (2018)

steps.action: Calibrate sigma_max (150-200 kPa) in 2007-2018 hindcasts for each forcing and q pair against observed 2017-2018 velocity and ice-front position, keeping three values per pair (Fig. S5, Table 1).
steps.quote: Values of σ max that minimized the misfit to observed surface velocities and ice front positions are in the range of 160–190 kPa

steps.action: Design the projection: minimum mass-loss runs (terminus held at 2017), control runs with 1960-1989 SMB to subtract drift, a 24-member perturbed parameter ensemble, q = 1 illustration runs, and four one-at-a-time sensitivity experiments (Table 2).
steps.quote: We later subtract this mass loss from the simulations in the perturbed parameter ensemble

steps.action: Estimate sea-level contribution from the observation-calibrated ensemble: 5.2-6.1 mm for minimum mass-loss runs and 6.2-8.7 mm for von Mises runs by 2100, relative to control (Figs. 4, 5).
steps.quote: Our von Mises calving scenarios predict 6.2–8.7 mm SLR from 2007–2100 relative to our control simulations

steps.action: Compare tuned-exponent runs with linear (q = 1) friction runs and find the tuned runs give up to twice the sea-level rise.
steps.quote: When compared with the linear basal friction law, our runs with tuned basal friction exponents predict up to twice as much SLR by 2100

steps.action: Report the model prediction that a sizable ice shelf grows by mid-century in all von Mises members and persists to 2100 except under HadGEM2.
steps.quote: We find that a significant amount of floating ice grows by the mid-century in all ensemble members using von Mises stress calving

steps.action: Decompose mass budgets, and deactivate undercutting in six 2007-2021 runs, showing that undercutting controls historical retreat through calving (Fig. S9).
steps.quote: We ran a set of six simulations from 2007–2021 with undercutting deactivated

steps.action: Run sensitivity experiments on ice-shelf removal in 2055 (+1-2 mm), sub-shelf melt tuning of 10/30 m/yr (<0.7 mm), and calving-rate caps of 1-7 km/yr and none (about 15% spread; no cap is unphysical).
steps.quote: We find that our assumptions about melt rates over the historical period have a small effect on our retreat projections

steps.action: Recognizing that the 3 km/yr cap may make the estimate conservative, run three low-sigma_max, 5 km/yr-cap simulations to set an upper bound on 2100 sea-level rise (Fig. S10).
steps.quote: We find an upper bound of ∼ 11–12 mm SLR, depending on climate forcing

steps.action: Repeat the optimization, q calibration and projections with BedMachine v3; the calibration needs q = 1/10-1/25 and gives up to 2 mm more sea-level rise (Fig. 10).
steps.quote: We find that for the version 3 bed, the model requires a considerably more plastic basal friction law to match the observed speedup

steps.action: Set results against Rignot et al. (2021), Carr et al. (2015), Choi et al. (2021) and ISMIP6, attributing the higher estimate mainly to the friction-law calibration.
steps.quote: Our estimated SLR contribution of 5.2–8.7 mm by 2100 is considerably higher than a recent estimate of ∼ 3.5 mm from Humboldt Glacier

steps.action: Reconcile the low calibrated sigma_max with Amaral et al.'s ~2 MPa and with ice tensile strength through auxiliary explanations (seasonal cycle, calving multiplier, calibration window), recasting sigma_max as a tuning parameter.
steps.quote: we posit that σ max should be seen as a tuning parameter without much physical significance

steps.action: Keep the claim that Humboldt will contribute significantly to sea-level rise this century, more than previously estimated, with ice dynamics possibly the dominant mass-budget term.
steps.quote: Humboldt Glacier is likely to make a significant contribution to SLR this century and that, to date, its potential contribution has been underestimated

sequences.source_document: Open discussion of tc-2022-20 (RC1, RC2, AC1/AC2 with response supplements)

steps.action: Both referees questioned separating the perturbed ensemble from the sensitivity tests and asked for a summary table; authors clarified the distinction (now §1 ¶3), added a summary table (Table 2) and moved the mesh convergence test to the supplement.
steps.page: RC1 ¶3; RC2 ¶4; AC1-S p.1; AC1-S p.6
steps.quote: We agree that the distinction between the perturbed parameter ensemble and the sensitivity experiments needs to be made more clear.

steps.action: Authors declined to move the bed-topography sensitivity test to an appendix, arguing it supports a main conclusion.
steps.quote: The bed topography sensitivity experiment we choose to keep in the main text

steps.action: Referee 1 asked why 1/5-1/7 was chosen when Fig. 3b favours other q in slow bands; authors explained the compromise across bands, promised clearer criteria and added a model-minus-observation panel (Fig. 3a).
steps.quote: We will also include a panel showing the difference between model and observations, either in Fig 3 or in the supplement.

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for details on melt depth translation and calving-front tracking; authors explained, and the text now describes front tracking and removal of calved ice (§2.5 ¶2).
steps.quote: The calving front is defined as the last cell with ice (either floating or grounded) that is adjacent to ocean open ocean

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for a quantitative assessment of initializing with other (summer) velocity products; authors declined new runs as too expensive and expanded the discussion of winter velocities (§4.1 ¶2).
steps.quote: Providing a truly quantitative assessment of the impact would require another initialization of the model and set of forward runs

steps.action: Referee 2 questioned the assumptions in the mu recalculation for each q; authors clarified effective pressure and offered diagnostic 2007 velocity solutions for each q, which appear as the Fig. S2 check (§2.3 ¶1).
steps.quote: we can easily corroborate the tuning procedure by showing diagnostic velocity solutions for the 2007 initial condition

steps.action: Authors declined to redo the inversion with 1/7 <= q <= 1/5 on cost grounds.
steps.quote: We have not re-done the inversion with 1/7≤q≤1/5 because it is too [...] .

steps.action: Referee 2 asked to calibrate q against the whole 2007-2017 record or seasonal velocities; authors defended decadal calibration against overfitting without new work.
steps.quote: We calibrated the basal friction law exponent for a decade of velocity change rather than to each year in the hindcasting period

steps.action: Referee 2 asked how the imposed retreat was converted to calving and whether submarine melt was active; authors explained, and the text now states this (§2.3 ¶1; §2.5 ¶2).
steps.quote: The imposed retreat rates are simply calculated from the difference between the observed 2007 and 2018 margin positions

steps.action: Asked about the control climatology, authors ran controls with a 1995-2005 MIROC5 climatology (control rises from ~0.85 to ~1.5 mm); this test is not reported in the published text.
steps.quote: We have explored using a 1995–2005 climatology from the MIROC5 model for both the q=⅕ and q=1/7 cases.

steps.action: Authors declined to repeat the sub-shelf melt test with MIROC5, citing the bounding cases.
steps.quote: We chose to do this for the bounding mass loss cases, and it turns out to not make a big difference for either

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for volume above flotation and sea-level equivalent in the calving-limit figure; authors added it (Fig. 9a).
steps.quote: Yes, we will add this.

steps.action: Authors declined a summary figure comparing all runs with previous estimates.
steps.quote: Sea-level rise estimates from previous studies are not easily available, so we choose not to attempt to include these in the figure.

tree.answer: Yes: documented 21st-century retreat and speedup of Humboldt Glacier
No: the future sea-level contribution must be inferred from a calibrated model
Estimate the likely range of sea-level rise by 2100 and its uncertainty sources
Yes: candidate basal friction exponents (linear and 1/3 versus semi-plastic) and calving thresholds
Yes: each q predicts a different 2017-2018 velocity field and sea-level rise
Set in the model (imposed retreat, forcings); observations found over one decade

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: one glacier, one decade; a 2015-2016 snapshot is the only second calibration
Partly: robust to melt tuning; sensitive to bed topography (+25%) and calving cap (up to 30%)
Kept: 5.2-8.7 mm by 2100; semi-plastic bed required
Yes, with clarifications; several requests declined

end.claim: Humboldt Glacier will likely contribute 5.2-8.7 mm to sea level by 2100 (6.2-8.7 mm with von Mises calving, 5.2-6.1 mm minimum), above earlier estimates, because transient calibration requires a semi-plastic friction law with q between 1/7 and 1/5.

decisive_move.sentence: The transient calibration of the basal friction exponent against the observed 2007-2018 speedup (steps 8-10) produces the semi-plastic q range that, by the authors' account, drives the larger estimate.

gates.evidence: All data are existing archives (velocity mosaics, BedMachine, OMG CTD, ISMIP6 forcings); no acquisition was directed by a hypothesis. The calibration step could have failed: candidate q values were scored against observed 2017-2018 velocities and the commonly used 1/3-1 fit poorly (§2.3 ¶2). The 2100 projection itself faces no test it could fail. Velocity bands and the selection of q were chosen after seeing the misfits and are called 'somewhat subjective' (§2.3 ¶2); nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: PDE-constrained adjoint optimization to invert for the basal friction field
finite-element/finite-volume solver (MPAS, Albany) for first-order Stokes
von Mises stress yield criterion used as calving law
tensile strength of ice (Petrovic 2003) as reference for sigma_max

novelty_claims.quote: Further, transient calibration of these parameterizations, which has not typically been performed, is necessary to reproduce observed behavior.
Our simulations predict 5.2–8.7 mm of sea-level rise from Humboldt Glacier, significantly higher than a previous estimate ( ∼ 3.5 mm)
to date, its potential contribution has been underestimated

limits: The estimate is a 24-member perturbed-parameter range, not a probability distribution; the sensitivity tests are one-at-a-time and are not propagated into the range (§2.6.3, AC1-S p.9). Uncertainty in the inverted friction field mu is not explored, nor is the structural choice of friction law beyond q = 1 illustration runs (§4.3 ¶2-3). The seasonal velocity cycle and ice-shelf hydrofracture are not modeled, and the 3 km/yr calving cap is ad hoc. The 2100 projection cannot be verified within the paper. Sub-claims and their statuses: the q range 1/7-1/5 is an estimate_with_resolution tied to BMv4 (q = 1/10-1/25 with BMv3); undercutting controlling historical retreat through calving is a best_explanation from an ablation; mid-century ice-shelf growth is a model prediction the authors call robust but sensitive to the calving cap (status best_explanation at most); the 11-12 mm upper bound is an estimate_with_resolution. Review process: a control-climatology test (1995-2005) run during review is not reported in the published text, and the mesh convergence test sits only in the supplement. Inference: the 2015-2016 recalibration (Fig. S4) may have been added during revision in response to Referee 2's request for further verification, but the record does not say so.

disagreements.target: Choi et al. (2021), ~3.5 mm from Humboldt Glacier
disagreements.support: The paper's calibrated ensemble gives 5.2-8.7 mm, and its own linear-friction runs give 4-5 mm, attributing the gap to Choi et al.'s linear-viscous law and lack of hindcast calibration.
disagreements.quote: Our estimated SLR contribution of 5.2–8.7 mm by 2100 is considerably higher than a recent estimate of ∼ 3.5 mm from Humboldt Glacier

disagreements.target: Commonly used linear-viscous and Weertman (q = 1/3) friction laws in ISMIP6 and ABUMIP models
disagreements.support: The q calibration shows exponents of 1/3-1 cannot reproduce the observed speedup at Humboldt.
disagreements.quote: both the linear-viscous and Weertman laws are still widely used for ice-sheet-scale simulations, despite being largely inappropriate for representing fast ice flow

disagreements.support: Tuned exponents double mass loss relative to linear friction, so models using linear or Weertman laws may underestimate (stated conditionally).
disagreements.quote: the ISMIP6 projections from models using linear or Weertman basal friction relationships may systematically underestimate 21st century retreat and mass loss

disagreements.target: Rignot et al. (2021): retreat driven by undercutting
disagreements.support: Mass budgets and the undercutting-off runs show that undercutting acts through calving rather than directly dominating mass loss.
disagreements.quote: However, the amount of submarine melt does not directly dominate the retreat as found by Rignot et al. (2021).

disagreements.target: Carr et al. (2015): submarine melt a small contribution; q = 1/3
disagreements.support: The undercutting ablation (Fig. S9) shows melt is important, and the calibration requires q of 1/7-1/5 rather than 1/3.
disagreements.quote: we have found that submarine melt is in fact an important factor in the retreat of Humboldt Glacier

disagreements.target: Amaral et al. (2020): sigma_max ~2 MPa at Humboldt
disagreements.support: The authors reconcile their calibrated value of 200 kPa or less through differences in calibration window, seasonal timing and the missing calving-multiplier physics.
disagreements.quote: Our simulations using the von Mises stress calving law require σ max ≤ 200 kPa in order for Humboldt Glacier to retreat

disagreements.target: Reading sigma_max as ice tensile strength (Petrovic, 2003)
disagreements.support: Calibrated values fall far below laboratory tensile strengths, so sigma_max is recast as a tuning parameter.
disagreements.quote: [...] may not fall within the reported range of ice tensile strength

disagreements.target: Practice of calving all floating ice immediately (e.g., Morlighem et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: Hindcasts that remove floating ice retreat too fast over the observed period.
disagreements.quote: We find that removing all floating ice leads to too rapid retreat over the observed period

disagreements.target: Previous modeling studies of Humboldt using older bed geometry
disagreements.support: The BMv3 runs require a different q and give up to 2 mm more sea-level rise, showing bed data affect projections.
disagreements.quote: previous modeling studies (Carr et al., 2015; Goelzer et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2021) may be hampered by inaccurate bed geometry

alternatives_considered.reason: largest velocity-change signal; avoids noisy interannual variability and data-gap aliasing
